text:
मोदी जी द्वारा दिए गए कल डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने झूठे विचार रखे जिनकी पोल खुल चुकी है।
दिल्ली में पत्रकारों, यू ट्यूबर,सोशल मीडिया एक्टिविस्ट को पीटा गिरफ्तार किया गया, सोशल मीडिया एकाउंट बंद किए जा रहे है लगातार।

कंपनियां हर महीने भारत सरकार को अपनी 'मासिक अनुपालन रिपोर्ट' (Monthly Compliance Report) सौंपती हैं
Facebook और Instagram (Meta): मेटा ने भारत के अन्दर 6 महीनों में 1.6 लाख (160,000) से अधिक अकाउंट्स पर सीधे बड़ी कार्रवाई की है।
• ट्विटर (X एक्स: एक महीने की अवधि में ही भारत में 5 लाख से अधिक अकाउंट्स को पूरी तरह बैन किया है। जिनमें कुछ समाचार पोर्टल और पत्रकारों के हैंडल भी शामिल थे।

गृह मंत्रालय के 'सहयोग पोर्टल' (Sahyog Portal) और IT एक्ट की धाराओं के तहत मार्च से जुलाई 2026 के बीच करीब 1.95 लाख (195,000) कंटेंट ब्लॉकिंग और टेकडाउन आदेश जारी किए गए। यह औसतन हर 68 सेकंड में एक आदेश के बराबर है।
• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

text:
I have filed a complaint with the Grievance Officer of YouTube against those bloggers as per the IT Rules, as directed by the Delhi High Court. The time limit for the Grievance Officer to act on the complaint is 15 days from the date of receipt. text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s announcement of a tax holiday from FY 2026-27 to FY 2067-2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services using Indian data centres has been interpreted as a reassurance to hyperscalers worried about permanent establishment risk. On the surface, that reading is correct. However, a deeper look reveals that the development masks a more interesting economic dynamic. 

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s announcement of a tax holiday from FY 2026-27 to FY 2067-2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services using Indian data centres has been interpreted as a reassurance to hyperscalers worried about permanent establishment risk. On the surface, that reading is correct.

However, a deeper look reveals that the development masks a more interesting economic dynamic. This measure will reshape the sharing of additional profits across the entire cloud value chain in India, benefiting not just the foreign tech giants, but also domestic data centre operators, Indian resellers, and—in ways often overlooked—Indian and global customers of cloud services.

The Budget 2026 exemption, on the face of it, applies to any foreign company earning “by procuring data centre services from a specified data centre” in India, with an exemption valid till March 2047. On first read, it seems to be a comfort measure for multinational companies such as AWS (Amazon), Microsoft, Google and Meta. Following several Supreme Court of India rulings, these companies feared that locating substantial infrastructure in India would trigger permanent establishment status, thus exposing them to Indian taxation on their global cloud revenues.

But here is the underlying operative constraint—the data centre must be owned and operated by an Indian company, notified under an approved scheme by the IT ministry. And, any sales to Indian customers must flow through an Indian reseller entity, typically the Indian subsidiary of the cloud firm or a domestic partner, which remains fully taxable in India with a 15 per cent safe harbour margin on costs.

What the Budget has done, in other words, is to trade away a potential tax claim on foreign cloud income in exchange for irreversible hard investment on Indian soil. The foreign company pays zero tax on a particular income stream; India ensures that data centre ownership, reseller involvement and domestic value-addition remain tethered to domestic companies, with massive, high-cost infrastructure on Indian soil.

Who benefits, and why the sequencing matters 

The primary beneficiary, as intended, is the foreign hyperscaler. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Meta have collectively announced around $67.5 billion of data centre and AI-related investments in India over the next five years. The tax holiday reduces their after-tax cost of using Indian capacity relative to hosting the same workloads in Singapore, the UAE or Europe, making India far more competitive for global cloud workloads. 

But the chain reaction begins here. The foreign cloud’s improved after-tax return immediately raises its willingness-to-pay for Indian data centre capacity. In a market where power, cooling and suitable land are scarce—as India races to build gigawatt-scale compute infrastructure—that willingness-to-pay gets reflected in higher lease rates and better contract terms negotiated with Indian data centre operators.

Those operators are India’s emerging infrastructure barons—AdaniConneX (targeting 1 GW capacity), Reliance Jio, Tata group platforms, Airtel’s Nxtra (commanding 15 per cent market share), Yotta Infrastructure, CtrlS, Sify and others. They are racing to create AI-ready facilities across Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Visakhapatnam, Noida and Pune. The tax holiday does not directly benefit them—they continue to pay corporate tax as usual—but it indirectly bolsters their negotiating position and pricing power by making foreign customers more willing to pay premium rates for access to “specified” notified facilities.

In global data centre markets, lease rates have risen sharply over 2023–2025 because AI and cloud demand have outstripped available power and cooling and, of course, high-performance GPUs. India’s operators, now assured that their primary foreign customers enjoy long-duration tax certainty, can capture a meaningful share of the additional profits generated by this bold income tax holiday through higher capacity pricing, coming on top of India’s ambitious Superconductor Mission, which envisages up to 50 per cent open-ended capital subsidy for domestic manufacturing of GPUs.

The reseller ecosystem and cloud customers 

The Budget structure mandates that Indian reseller entities—AWS India, Microsoft India, Google Cloud India, cloud arms of IT majors like TCS, Infosys and Wipro, and telecom-embedded providers—be part of the sales chain when claiming the exemption for Indian customer sales. The 15 per cent safe harbour rules, also a part of this Budget, on related-party data centre service costs signal policy comfort with a layered value chain and protect reseller margins.

Indian and global consumers of cloud services—startups, SMEs, enterprises and SaaS firms—stand to benefit from the competitive intensity that this tax holiday catalyses. As competition among hyperscalers deepens and capacity expands, some of the additional profits will pass through as more competitive cloud pricing, lowering barriers to digital adoption and improving margins for businesses reliant on India-hosted infrastructure. 

The political economy of how this is presented matters. Announcing a “tax holiday for foreign cloud providers till 2047 reads as a necessary course correction; announcing what the opposition could frame as “20-year tax holiday for data centre conglomerates like Adani, Reliance and Tata” would draw harsher scrutiny. By routing the direct benefit through the foreign entity while hard-wiring Indian ownership, the government has elegantly packaged a very substantial infrastructure incentive inside a narrative of global openness.

This is a political skill. But it is worth being explicit: the Budget’s measure is as much about anchoring hard assets and Indian ownership as it is about welcoming foreign clouds.

Why long-term certainty was necessary

There is, however, a compelling policy case—and indeed, this bold and substantial income tax holiday is quite justified. Data centres are the physical backbone of cloud computing and AI. As workloads grow heavier, hosting capacity within national borders becomes a question of digital sovereignty. India has already moved in that direction through data localisation norms and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

The Budget’s tax holiday is a fiscal complement to that regulatory thrust: it says to foreign clouds, “Bring compute and workloads to India; we will not use the tax system to ambush you”—but Indian ownership and domestic intermediaries remain non-negotiable.

Viewed this way, the measure is not a disguised giveaway but a conscious, well-crafted and necessary concession: India forgoes contested tax claims in exchange for encouraging irreversible hard investment, in the order of billions of dollars, on Indian soil. That is reasonable for a country betting on becoming a global cloud hub and a centre of AI capability. 

The winners are multiple: foreign hyperscalers gain tax certainty; Indian data centre operators gain pricing power and volume; Indian resellers gain regulated margins and market growth; cloud customers gain access to cheaper, more competitive services anchored in India. It is a policy that aligns incentives across the entire value chain while preserving domestic ownership and taxable profit pools.

The packaging is clever. The economics are sound.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

The Union government’s draft Seeds Bill 2025, now open for public comments until 11 December, arrives not a day too soon. From counterfeit packets in village markets to procurement disputes at mandis, the chain between breeder and farmer has too many weak links.

For Punjab, where seed quality, FCI norms, and groundwater stress intersect, if not collide, every season, this Bill is more than a compliance document. It is a chance to rebuild trust in the most basic input of agriculture.

How is it better than the old law?

Three design shifts from the Seeds Act of 1966 deserve unambiguous support.

First, universal registration of varieties. The 1966 Act essentially regulated only ‘notified’ kinds, leaving a grey market of truthfully labelled seeds outside meaningful oversight. The draft moves toward mandatory registration for all new varieties and a pathway for deemed registration of existing ones. If implemented with predictable timelines and transparent criteria, this closes the back door through which poor-quality seed has circulated for decades.

Second, traceability and digital oversight. The draft emphasises traceability— already feasible through platforms that assign a scannable identity to each lot from breeder to dealer. That lets a farmer verify authenticity at the counter and allows regulators to trace a bad lot swiftly up the chain. Traceability should not be a slogan; it must become a farmer’s everyday tool. Make it mandatory at scale, standardise the QR/barcode, and integrate it with e-invoices so that one scan reveals who produced, processed, stored, and sold the seed, and when.

Third, smarter penalties with measured decriminalisation. Minor technical lapses should not land honest actors in criminal court; serious fraud should. The draft’s graded penalties, with steep fines and custodial terms for spurious and unregistered seed, are a clear improvement over the token fines of the 1966 law. The promise is a system that is both business-friendly and farmer‑protective—if enforcement stays sharp.

Two related moves are consequential for Punjab. One is the shift from a state-by-state dealer licensing culture to centralised accreditation/recognition. That may cut duplication for multi-state firms, but it also risks hollowing out the “last mile” unless states retain day-to-day inspection teeth. The other is price oversight “in emergent situations”. That clause matters in the sowing window, when speculation can shut smallholders out of quality seed.

Federal design at the last mile

The August ruling of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which held that states cannot ban centrally notified hybrid paddy, was a reminder that seed regulation sits across the Centre-state seam. Punjab has since hardened deterrence at its end, making the sale of spurious seeds a non-bailable, cognisable offence, reflecting accumulated anger in the countryside at fly-by-night operators. Industry protests aside, the message from Chandigarh is clear: the deterrent must be felt in the marketplace.

The draft national law should recognise this reality instead of flattening it. Keep national registration and central accreditation if you must—but codify concurrent enforcement powers for states: surprise sampling, seizure, prosecution, and the ability to prescribe local storage and display conditions. Delhi can set standards; inspectors in Moga and Muktsar will enforce them.

Farmers’ vantage point: performance and procurement

From a farmer’s field, regulation is judged by three blunt questions: Did the seed perform? If not, who pays? And will the crop be procured on fair terms?

The draft is strong at the pre-market gate (registration and traceability) and on deterrence. It is notably weaker on compensation when registered seed underperforms despite adoption of the recommended package of practices. Punjab’s last two seasons underlined why this gap matters: disruptive weather, discolouration and moisture contests at mandis, and a milling reluctance toward some hybrids have turned quality disputes into income shocks.

The fix is straightforward. Create a time-bound, no-fault compensation window for clear seed failures, financed by a blend of mandatory manufacturer insurance, a small cess on registrations, and state top-ups in disaster years. Publish the yield-loss formula up front; do not force a small farmer to litigate against a corporate legal team. At the same time, institutionalise pre-season coordination among the Agriculture Ministry, FCI/DFPD, and states on uniform procurement specifications, with a hybrid-specific annexure and pre-declared relaxations for flood years. Let seed standards and procurement norms talk to each other before the first bag is sold.

Let FPOs co-brand seed

Earlier seed‑bill drafts recognised a farmer’s right to save, use, exchange and sell farm‑saved seed, with one caveat: it cannot be sold under a brand name.

The intent was to block quasi‑commercial masquerading without quality assurance. But the rise of Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) changes the calculus. The Union government wants FPOs to aggregate, process, and market produce; it funds them and extends credit and tax support for precisely that reason. If the final Seeds Act mechanically extends a “no brand” caveat to FPO‑aggregated seed, it would hobble a flagship reform.

The harmonising path is clear: permit FPO co-branding of farm-saved seed provided three conditions are met. First, lots must pass notified minimum standards in an accredited lab. Second, full traceability, including grower IDs and storage logs that must be uploaded to the national portal. Third, liability must sit with the FPO’s board for false claims, not with individual members. That keeps out fly-by-night branding while letting farmer institutions move up the value chain.

Dealer liability, without scapegoating the honest

Punjab has thousands of small input dealers who act as the farmer’s first line of advice and supply. They cannot become the system’s whipping boy for failures they did not cause.

The law should adopt a manufacturer-first liability rule on germination and genetic purity for factory-sealed packs, while giving dealers a safe harbour if they sell sealed lots, meet prescribed storage conditions, keep traceable invoices, and hand over required samples during inspections. Penal exposure should bite dealers who tamper, knowingly misbrand, or operate outside the accredited chain. That keeps deterrence where it belongs—on those who cheat—without driving legitimate retailers out of business.

Traceability as a price stabiliser, not just a cop’s tool

If the Centre retains emergency price-control powers, anchor them in transparent triggers captured by the traceability system: inventory-to-sowing-window ratios, abnormal interstate price spreads, and unusual movement patterns. Public dashboards would discipline prices before official fiat is needed, and they would help states intervene in time. Let the QR on a packet be both a shield against fraud and a signal for markets.

Water‑wise seed choices backed by procurement

For Punjab, seed policy is also water policy. Short-duration, water-efficient paddy, as well as non-paddy kharif options, must get fast-track registration and agronomy support.

But farmers will not switch varieties or crops unless procurement policy aligns. That means assured purchase pathways for water-saving options, predictable miller acceptance for hybrids, and extension support that links seed choice to groundwater outcomes. Otherwise, the rational farmer will cling to long-duration staples that mills prefer and FCI buys on familiar specs.

It is essential to stitch seed regulation to FCI procurement policy for hybrid paddy so that what farmers sow confidently in June is not rejected quibblingly in October.

Minor tweaks before enactment: a Punjab‑first checklist

Keep central registration, but write state enforcement powers into the statute.

Clarify the liability chain: manufacturer first; dealer safe harbour for sealed, properly stored, traceable stock; strict penalties for tampering and misbranding.

Make compensation real with a time‑bound, no‑fault window and a published formula.

Hard‑wire coordination with FCI on uniform specs and a hybrid‑specific annexure, with pre‑declared relaxations in disaster years.

Use traceability to improve competition and price discovery, not merely to police.

Greenlight FPO co‑branding under standards‑plus‑traceability, with board‑level liability.

Invest in accredited seed labs and risk‑based inspections so enforcement is fast, fair and science‑led.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Every week someone tells me they vibe-coded their app over the weekend and don't need developers anymore.

Before it touches a paying customer, make sure it includes:

> a schema someone designed, instead of one the AI improvised table by table
> login that still works when someone puts a plus sign in their email
> password reset links that expire and work once
> MFA, plus a recovery path for the user who lost their phone
> sessions that time out, and a way to kill every session for one user
> SSO for the enterprise customer who won't sign without it
> SAML, because that customer's IT team doesn't do magic links
> SCIM, so a fired employee loses access the moment IT offboards them
> roles and permissions deeper than "admin" and "everyone else"
> checks that stop user A from reading user B's data by changing one number in the URL
> tenant isolation, so one customer's bug never shows another customer's records
> an admin "log in as this user" button for support, with an audit trail on every use
> rate limits on login, so nobody can guess passwords at scale
> lockouts that stop attackers without locking out your CFO the night before the board meeting
> database migrations that run forward and roll back
> migrations that don't lock the main table at 2pm on a Tuesday
> indexes, because the query that was instant on 50 test rows times out on 5 million real ones
> connection pooling, so a traffic spike doesn't exhaust the database
> backups every night
> a restore from those backups, tested, because a backup you've never restored is a hope
> point-in-time recovery for the day someone runs a delete without a where clause
> soft deletes, so "I deleted it by accident" is a support ticket and not an incident
> validation on the server, not just in the form
> timezones stored right, so the 9am reminder doesn't fire at 4am
> the customer with an apostrophe in their last name
> emoji, accents and right-to-left text in every field
> money stored as integers, because 0.1 + 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in floating point
> currency, rounding and tax rules for every country you sell into
> a data model that survives your second customer asking for "one small change"
> idempotency keys, so a retried payment doesn't charge the card twice
> deduplication for the user who clicks submit four times
> pagination that still works on page 400
> exports, because sooner or later every customer wants their data in a spreadsheet
> imports that survive the CSV someone saved in 2009
> retention rules, and code that deletes what your contract says you'll delete
> secrets out of the code, out of the repo and out of the AI chat history
> rotating every key the AI pasted into a config file last month
> confirming every package the AI installed exists and is the one you meant
> dependency scanning, because the AI pulled in libraries nobody reviewed
> input sanitization everywhere a user can type
> protection against SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and the rest of the OWASP list
> file uploads that get scanned, size-limited and stored where they can't execute
> CORS rules that aren't "allow everything"
> security headers on every response
> encryption at rest and in transit
> least-privilege access for everyone, including the AI agent holding production credentials
> logs that record who did what, without recording passwords, tokens or card numbers
> a penetration test before your enterprise customer's security team runs their own
> answers to the security questionnaire every enterprise buyer sends, with evidence behind each one
> a disclosure process for the day a stranger emails you a vulnerability
> a plan for the day a laptop with production access gets stolen
> SOC 2, which means policies, evidence and an auditor, not a checkbox
> HIPAA, the moment a single patient record touches your system
> a BAA with every vendor that touches that data, including your AI model provider
> audit trails that show who viewed a record, not just who changed it
> PCI scope, and card numbers kept out of your database
> GDPR deletion requests that reach every table, backup and log
> data residency for the customer whose contract says EU only
> quarterly access reviews someone signs off on
> dev, staging and production environments that match each other
> infrastructure written as code, so the setup lives somewhere other than one person's memory
> a deploy pipeline that runs the tests before anything reaches customers
> one-click rollbacks, because Friday deploys happen
> zero-downtime deploys, because your customers don't have maintenance windows
> feature flags, so you can ship the code without shipping the feature
> autoscaling for the Monday morning spike
> a CDN, so the app loads fast in Singapore too
> DNS, SSL certificates, and renewals that don't expire on a Sunday
> background job queues, so slow work doesn't freeze the page
> retries with backoff, so one flaky API call doesn't become a lost order
> a dead-letter queue for the jobs that fail every retry
> cron jobs that don't run twice the day you add a second server
> caching, and clearing that cache when the data changes
> SPF, DKIM and DMARC, so your password resets don't land in spam
> bounce and complaint handling on every transactional email
> storage rules, so you stop paying to keep 2021's temp files
> cost alerts, so a runaway agent loop shows up the same day and not on the invoice (we learned this one for $1,382.59)
> a disaster recovery plan, written down and tested once a year
> a second region, if your contract promises uptime one region can't deliver
> structured logs you can search at 3am
> error tracking that groups the same bug instead of sending you 4,000 emails
> uptime checks from outside your own network
> alerts that page a human, tuned until they stop paging for nothing
> dashboards for latency, error rate and throughput
> tracing for one slow request across every service it touches
> an on-call rotation, and a person who picks up
> runbooks, so the engineer on call knows what "queue depth critical" means
> postmortems that change something
> a status page customers check before they email you
> unit tests written by someone who knows what the logic should do
> integration tests for every third-party API you depend on
> end-to-end tests for signup, checkout and the other flows that make you money
> load testing before the launch email goes out
> test data that looks like production without being production data
> regression tests, so fixing bug 41 doesn't bring back bug 12
> testing on the five-year-old laptop your biggest customer's ops team still uses
> accessibility compliance, because the enterprise contract requires it
> subscriptions, upgrades, downgrades and proration
> failed-payment retries and dunning emails
> invoices with the customer's PO number on them, because procurement won't pay without it
> sales tax and VAT
> refunds, credits and partial refunds
> usage metering that matches what you bill, to the cent
> annual contracts with custom terms your billing logic never planned for
> revenue reports your finance team can reconcile
> webhooks that verify signatures
> webhooks that retry, with a log of every failed delivery
> a versioned API, so you can change it without breaking your customers' integrations
> API keys customers can create and revoke
> API rate limits that protect you without blocking real integrations
> a plan for the day a third-party API changes its response format without telling you
> OAuth token refresh, because tokens expire at the worst possible moment
> a sandbox where customers can test their integration
> protection against prompt injection in every field that reaches the model
> customer and patient data kept out of prompts that leave your network
> a model spend cap per customer, so one heavy user can't run up your bill
> evals, so you find out when a model update makes your answers worse
> a fallback for the afternoon your model provider goes down
> a migration plan for the day your model gets deprecated
> prompt and output logs for debugging, minus whatever you're not allowed to keep
> a human approval step for anything the AI does that can't be undone
> pages that load on hotel wifi
> empty states, loading states and error states on every screen
> error messages a customer can act on, instead of "something went wrong"
> forms that keep what people typed when one field fails validation
> emails that render in every mail client your customers use
> notifications people can turn off
> undo
> keyboard navigation and screen reader support
> translations, with dates and numbers formatted for each locale
> a back button that does what people expect
> code a human can read
> code review on every change
> a branching strategy, so two people can work without overwriting each other
> monthly dependency upgrades, so you're never two major versions behind
> framework upgrades before the old version stops getting security patches
> deleting the dead code the AI left behind from its first three attempts
> splitting up the 2,000-line file the AI kept appending to
> architecture decisions written down, with the reasons
> a README that gets a new engineer running locally in under an hour
> documentation for whoever inherits this
> an admin panel for your ops team
> support tooling, so customer success can answer questions without pinging engineering
> a changelog customers can read
> terms and a privacy policy that match what the code does
> every account, domain and repo in the company's name, not the name of whoever built the prototype
> a bus factor higher than one

Oh, and besides keeping all of this working every day, forever… your vibe-coded app will still need people who know what they're doing:

> reading every line the AI wrote before it ships (a senior engineer)
> designing the data model before your second customer breaks it (a backend engineer)
> explaining why the AI's fix for one bug created two new ones (a senior engineer, again)
> deploys, rollbacks, servers and the cloud bill (a DevOps engineer)
> answering the page at 3am when payments stop (whoever's on call)
> patching the framework the week a vulnerability goes public (security)
> walking an auditor through how patient data moves (security and compliance)
> testing what the AI says it tested (QA)
> running a migration on a live database without losing a row (a backend engineer)
> saying no to the feature that breaks three others (a tech lead)
> turning "works on my laptop" into "works for every customer at once" (an architect)
> debugging the code when the AI that wrote it can't (a senior engineer)
> remembering why it's built this way, a year from now (someone who was there)

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"
