"Hasan DemirkiranKontexthasan@kontext.securityJens ErnstbergerKontextjens@kontext.security
Abstract
AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions.
We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises.
We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard’s decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.
1Introduction
A benchmark may be easy for the wrong reason. Annotation conventions, source identity, repeated templates, and collection artifacts can all predict labels without measuring the intended construct (Gururangan et al., 2018; Geirhos et al., 2020). This problem is especially consequential for agent-safety evaluation. A tool guard may be deployed to approve or block a consequential action, while its benchmark record also contains scaffolding added by the evaluation pipeline: provenance tags, tool names, trajectory length, source subsets, and repeated interaction structure.Simple lexical and length features separated honest and attack trajectories in the public LinuxArena sample, motivating a search for analogous rules elsewhere. Such a rule may track real risk, collection differences, or evidence also used by a capable guard; rule–guard agreement cannot distinguish these https://t.co/vAy7xxijcb systematically uncover potential shortcuts, we introduce shortcut auditing as a three-level inference ladder for agent-safety guard evaluations. A shortcut audit asks progressively stronger questions: can a simple cue predict released labels; is that cue associated with guard decisions; and does changing only that cue alter the guard’s decision?We distinguish:1.Label Predictability: Can a deliberately capability-poor rule predict released labels?
2.Observational Guard Association: Do guard decisions correlate with the suspected cue in released records?
3.Paired Decision Sensitivity: Does the guard change when the cue is changed while the candidate action’s authorization and effect are held fixed?Paired edits test whether changing the input changes the guard’s decision. To interpret that change as spurious shortcut reliance, the edits must preserve the relevant safety information. For a deterministic guard, evaluating each original–edited pair reveals whether the strict decision changes. Stochastic guards require additional controls because identical inputs can produce different outputs and sequential calls may drift over time. We therefore interleave repeated original and edited calls, include a formatting placebo, and report identical-input disagreement separately.Our contributions are:•Three-level shortcut-audit framework. We introduce a inference ladder separating label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity with explicit construct-preservation caveats, plus repeat and placebo controls for stochastic guards.
•Audit of released agent-safety evaluations. We apply shortcut-auditing to AgentDojo-Traj, a LinuxArena public sample, and to AgentHarm-Traj. Across LinuxArena and two TS-Bench-derived datasets, we expose label separability, exact-tool domain-transfer failure, and evaluation-unit sensitivity: command length reaches AUC .910, exact- tool lookup falls from F1=.901 to .495 under domain holdout, and TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 to .719 under equal-interaction weighting.
•Guard-level shortcut validation. We move beyond showing that benchmark labels are predictable by testing candidate cues directly against guard decisions, using a purpose-built TS-Guard reproduction and hosted models configured as pre-execution guards. Repeated paired AgentDojo-Traj interventions with a placebo control reveal material Haiku sensitivity, while Luna and Q8 TS-Guard checks show that the effect is configuration-specific. Haiku blocking changes by −8.33 percentage points (pp) for the marker rewrite and +11.46​pp for aliases. With the same cohort, conditions, schedule, repetitions, and estimand, GPT-5.6 Luna gives 0.00​pp and +1.04​pp, while the deterministic TS-Guard reproduction changes its decision for 3 of 64 marker-edit pairs.The result is deliberately not “these benchmarks are broken.” Some proxies are intentional and semantically relevant: an untrusted-content marker communicates provenance, and a malicious request is relevant to a harm policy. Our claim is that such features create shortcut opportunities. Evaluation authors should measure whether conclusions survive group holdouts, equal-unit weighting, paired perturbations with construct-preservation caveats, and repeat-original controls. In this paper, shortcut auditing means testing whether apparent findings survive these checks.
2A three-level shortcut-audit framework
Let a benchmark record be x=(s,z). Here, s is the remaining context needed to judge the candidate action, such as the request, interaction history, tool description, and arguments. The variable z is the candidate cue singled out for audit (e.g. trajectory-length). This analytical decomposition does not assume that z is irrelevant or spurious. It tests how strongly a guard evaluation depends on the cue or on its representation. Let y be the released label, r⁡(z)∈ℝ a capability-poor diagnostic that does not observe s, and g⁡(x)∈{0,1} a guard decision, with one denoting block. Figure 1 summarizes the three claims and the inference licensed at each level.1. Label predictability
Does r⁡(z) predict y?
Finds a candidate cue.2. Observational guard
association
Does g⁡(s,z) vary with z?
Nominates an edit.3. Paired decision
sensitivity
Compare g⁡(s,z) with g⁡(s,z′).
Tests that exact edit.Figure 1: The three-level shortcut-audit framework. Each level motivates the next test, not the next conclusion. Paired edits probe decision sensitivity only to the extent that they preserve the target construct; stochastic guards additionally require repeat and placebo controls.

Level 1: label predictability.
We evaluate a deliberately capability-poor diagnostic r using only z, not the judgment context s. Its score isSpred​(r)=ℳ⁡({(r⁡(zi),yi)}i=1n),(1)where ℳ is an appropriate discrimination metric, such as AUC, F1, or balanced accuracy. Our diagnostics include command length, a marker plus a short verb list, exact tool lookup, and an all-positive baseline. Strong performance establishes a predictive construction signature. It does not show that the cue is spurious, available to a deployed guard, or used by that guard.
Level 2: observational guard association.
For an input-visible cue, let a⁡(z)∈{0,1} indicate whether the audited cue is present. Within a comparison cohort C, we measureΔassoc(C)=𝔼[g(x)∣a(z)=1,x∈C]−𝔼[g(x)∣a(z)=0,x∈C].(2)The cohort C can restrict comparisons to the same released label, domain, action family, or another matched context. A large contrast can nominate a cue for intervention. It remains observational because z, y, and legitimate evidence in s share a data-generating process, so measured and unmeasured confounding can explain the association.
Level 3: paired decision sensitivity.
For a deterministic guard and transformation T⁡(s,z)=(s,z′), we measure the paired strict-decision flip ratepflip(T)=1n∑i=1n[g(xi)≠g(T(xi))].(3)The intervention must preserve the label and intended construct; otherwise the flip may be legitimate. For stochastic g, the target estimand is insteadΔT=1n∑i=1n{Pr[g(T(xi))=1]−Pr[g(xi)=1]},(4)estimated here by repeated calls in both conditions. Under stable independent draws, the signed K=1 mean g⁡(T⁡(xi))−g⁡(xi) is unbiased for ΔT, but can be imprecise and temporally confounded when calls are not interleaved. Its unsigned flip rate is a different, descriptive disagreement estimand. Independent repeat disagreement measures stability and should not be subtracted from either quantity. A strict-decision non-flip also does not exclude changes in ordinal scores, components, rationales, or redundant feature use.This ladder combines ideas from shortcut learning, group-shift evaluation, behavioral testing, and contrast sets (Geirhos et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). Our contribution is to operationalize label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity as a three-level audit for released agent-safety evaluations. The experiments show that strong label predictability can coexist with localized paired decision sensitivity.
3Evaluation artifacts and audit design

3.1Evaluation artifacts

LinuxArena.
LinuxArena evaluates control protocols for agents operating in live software environments (Tracy et al., 2026). We use the 932-row public sample at a pinned dataset revision. Of these, 918 rows contain extracted shell commands. Because the public sample repeats action traces under different monitor runs, we hash complete action content after removing only the monitor response. The primary diagnostic contains 576 exact-action-unique shell trajectories: 176 attack and 400 honest across ten environments. We never use the nominally unique trajectory_id as a deduplication key. The sample also contains LinuxArena’s precomputed per-action suspicion scores from its Claude Opus 4.6 monitor on 200 Opus-generated honest trajectories and 74 human-crafted LaStraj attacks. The monitor conditions on the task, possible side-task goals, and tool-call history, but not agent reasoning; each stored score averages two calls.
TS-Bench.
ToolSafe introduces TS-Bench and TS-Guard for pre-execution, step-level tool safety (Mou et al., 2026). TS-Bench derives the released AgentDojo-Traj and AgentHarm-Traj step records, including step-level risk scores, from AgentDojo and AgentHarm trajectories (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025). We use these files at a pinned commit; the paired AgentDojo-Traj variants described below are the only new inputs we construct. Under ToolSafe’s strict mapping, every nonzero risk rating is unsafe. AgentDojo-Traj has 1,220 steps (352 unsafe and 868 safe) across four domains. AgentHarm-Traj has 731 steps (525 unsafe and 206 safe) in 197 released interaction-ID groups.We use released labels, TS-Guard predictions, and previously cached hosted-guard assessments from pinned source commits. No tool call in a record is executed. The appendix gives a PDF-contained reproduction specification. The aggregate code/results package is publicly available.11https://github.com/hasandemirkiran/shortcut-sensitivity-agent-safety-evaluations It contains no raw benchmark text, arguments, identifiers, or provider responses.
Audit scope.
Here, an audit means applying the three-level framework in Section 2 to released evaluation artifacts. We test whether simple cues predict labels, whether input-visible cues are associated with guard decisions, and, when an edit intended to preserve the construct is available, whether paired edits change those decisions. The analysis is black-box: it uses released records, outputs, and fixed input transformations without access to guard internals. We do not test an adaptive agent, an evasion attack, or end-to-end tool execution.
3.2Capability-poor diagnostics
Level 1 begins with one deliberately limited diagnostic matched to each artifact’s construction. The aim is not to build the best classifier. It is to test whether a narrow cue recovers released labels and whether that result survives controls for duplication, source overlap, transfer, and evaluation-unit weighting. For LinuxArena, the deterministic score is the negative mean shell-command character count, so larger scores indicate shorter commands. We compare it with character n-gram TF–IDF and logistic regression trained leave-one-environment-out (LOEO). We report AUC and a clustered bootstrap over main-task/side-task groups. These are completed-trajectory diagnostics, not operational step-wise monitors.For AgentDojo-Traj, the fixed binary rule requires both the literal <INFORMATION> marker in history and a current tool whose name starts with one of 11 side-effect verbs (for example, send_, delete_, or update_). The rule and verb list were frozen after initial inspection, so this is a diagnostic audit rather than a preregistered test. A second diagnostic memorizes each exact tool’s majority label. For unseen tool names, it predicts the training fold’s overall majority label; ties are classified as unsafe. We evaluate it both with interaction- grouped five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-domain-out (LODO) transfer. The lookup explicitly uses evaluation labels and must not be described as a deployable classifier.For AgentHarm-Traj, we test the all-unsafe baseline and audit the mapping from source subset to strict label. We then recompute guard metrics at three units: rows, equal-weight interactions, and one majority prediction per interaction. This distinguishes performance over recorded steps from performance over underlying tasks. Separately, we case-fold parsed tool names, normalize their structured arguments, retain exact-execution groups containing both labels, and compare safe and unsafe context means with equal weight per execution group.
3.3Frozen AgentDojo counterfactual cohort
A frozen cohort is a fixed panel of base steps and paired edits selected before any guard is run on the edited inputs. Freezing prevents us from choosing examples after seeing intervention outcomes; pairing holds the underlying step fixed; and balancing eight marker-present safe and eight marker-present unsafe steps from each AgentDojo domain prevents one domain or label from dominating. This deterministic selection produces 64 bases from 58 source interactions. “Frozen” does not mean preregistered or representative of the full benchmark: released labels and earlier guard outputs had already been inspected. Each base has an original; a marker rewrite replacing <INFORMATION> with <UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL_CONTENT> (and the matching closing tag) while retaining enclosed content; a consistent opaque tool alias retaining description and arguments; and their combination. The hosted run adds a neutral placebo that changes only outer JSON whitespace. Operational-action and label preservation were intended edit constraints, not independently established facts: we performed no blinded human equivalence check. The marker rewrite makes untrusted external provenance more explicit, while the aliases are generated separately for each sample and do not represent one globally consistent tool renaming, so the estimand is sensitivity to these exact edits rather than proof of spurious use. Within this study, marker rewrite versus original is the focal edit; alias and combined edits are exploratory stress tests.
Guards.
Our deterministic subject is a byte-pinned 8-bit, group-64 MLX reproduction of the public TS-Guard checkpoint under greedy decoding. It passes a predeclared gate on the 64 originals: 64/64 parse, 63/64 strict decisions and 58/64 exact scores agree with the release. This result applies only to that Q8/MLX reproduction, not the released BF16/vLLM execution path.We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025) as a prompted stochastic guard. In a seven-configuration observational screen, it had the largest safe-row marker association (74.09​pp), making it a high-association case for paired intervention. Selection used cached observational outputs; the 64-step cohort and edits were fixed before the 960 new intervention calls. Table 3 reports the full screen. We make three deterministically interleaved calls per base and condition (960 total), at temperature zero with structured outputs, routing only to Anthropic through OpenRouter with fallback disabled. The primary estimand averages each base’s three-call block-probability difference, with 10,000 domain-stratified bootstrap replicates clustered over the 58 source interactions. The formatting placebo and within-condition disagreement diagnose serialization sensitivity and instability. After the Haiku result, but before inspecting any valid Luna outcome, we added GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026) as a compact cross-provider replication. It uses the same cohort, prompt, five conditions, three calls per condition, and normalized base/condition/repetition order. We route only to OpenAI through OpenRouter with fallback disabled, request medium reasoning and structured output, and apply the same estimand and bootstrap. This replication tests cross-model generality; it is not a model-strength comparison. A secondary one-draw GPT-5.5 check is reported in Appendix C; it is not part of the repeated primary analysis.

4Predictive benchmark cues are strong

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

The Election Commission restricted public access to election CCTV footage in December 2024, reduced its retention period to 45 days in May 2025, and now admits it has no records of how many requests for such footage it received over five years.  

Independent scrutiny of the electoral process is the need of time.  

Democracy demands transparency, accountability and verifiable evidence #VoteChori

This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Watch this advertisement carefully. It clearly conveys the message that if the government has failed to deliver good governance, the citizens have the power to change it through elections.

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

And now we are witnessing something even more disturbing.

Instead of concentrating on enrolling every eligible citizen, the electoral roll revision has resulted in the removal of approximately 13 crore names. Genuine voters are being forced to struggle to establish their eligibility and recover their voting rights.

With an adult population exceeding 100 crore, the Election Commission must explain how many eligible citizens remain outside the electoral rolls and how many have been wrongly excluded.

The Election Commission’s constitutional responsibility is to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote, not to make citizens struggle to protect their existing voting rights.

Look at the complete reversal.

Earlier, the Election Commission encouraged citizens to vote, expanded participation and introduced measures to strengthen public confidence.

IEC enters into partnership to counter disinformation | @SAgovnews

October 20, 2026

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has entered into a partnership with Google, Meta, Microsoft, TikTok and non-profit organisation, Moxii Africa, to ensure the integrity of election information and counter disinformation ahead of the 4 November 2026 Local Government Elections.

The partnership is a sequel to a similar framework signed with the platforms ahead of the 2024 National and Provincial Elections (NPE). It is an indispensable lever buttressing the Commission’s purposive measures to enhance the integrity of election information.

These measures include the gazetting of the Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections (the Disinformation Code), on 4 September 2026.

The Code applies to political parties, candidates and anyone acting on their behalf. It forms part of the Electoral Code of Conduct and carries the same sanctions. 

According to the Commission, the partnership brings the platforms into the same effort to keep election information accurate and trustworthy.

Underscoring the importance of the partnership, the Commission’s Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo said the strategic inclusion of the online platforms gives the Commission direct access to the platforms and a real fighting chance against disinformation.

“Our partnership with digital platforms is critical to ensuring that voters have access to credible, accurate and trustworthy information to make informed political choices. A technically flawless election can still lose public trust if citizens are overwhelmed by disinformation.

“Therefore, the partnership eliminates barriers to direct access to the platforms and enables instantaneous remedial action against disinformation peddlers,” Mamabolo said.

The partnership covers the following:
• Cooperation in good faith during the election period;
• Respect for existing laws, with no requirement to share confidential user data;
• Alignment with the Constitution, municipal electoral laws and the Electoral Code of Conduct, including the Disinformation Code;
• A working group of partners, election awareness campaigns, and training on disinformation for political parties, candidates and other stakeholders;
• Room for platforms to apply their own policies, including content removal, advisory warnings and delisting, and
• Cooperation on other initiatives intended to curb the impact of disinformation in elections.
 The Commission has designated the Real411 platform to support its proactive efforts to minimise the impact of disinformation during the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Anyone who sees suspected election-related disinformation can report it to Real411 at https://t.co/Kc7kXVrgbE or through the Real411 app.

Complaints are handled in all eleven official languages. Real411 assesses complaints independently and recommends action to the Commission and the platforms.

Depending on the findings, the Commission, upon careful review of any reported complaint indicating disinformation or misinformation, can: 
• Refer the matter to the Electoral Court, which can impose sanctions. 
• Promptly refer the matter to the relevant online platform, which is expected to prioritise referrals from the Commission by acknowledging and swiftly processing the notification in line with its policies. 
• Issue media statements to alert the public and correct the disinformation. Guidance for voters on spotting, checking and reporting disinformation is available at https://t.co/7XX2mAKHXp.

The partners welcomed the partnership and reaffirmed their commitment to working with the Commission. They noted that they already have policies and mechanisms to counter disinformation and will keep using them as part of the collective effort.

“Free, fair and credible elections depend on people being able to trust the information they see. No single organisation can tackle disinformation alone, which is why Microsoft is pleased to join the Electoral Commission in this partnership.

“Ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, we will work alongside the Commission, civil society and industry to help voters find authoritative election information, strengthen media and AI literacy, and counter deceptive AI-generated content,” said Director: Government Affairs, Microsoft South Africa, Abongile Vanda in affirming Microsoft’s support for the partnership.

“At TikTok, we recognise the important role our platform plays in helping people discover information and engage in public conversations. This is why we take our responsibility to protect our community during elections very seriously.

“Through our in-app Election Centre, South Africans will be able to access reliable information about the elections, and to further support this, we have introduced election-related labels and search banners that direct users to the centre with a single tap.

“This work is supported by advanced moderation, collaboration with fact-checking partners and electoral commissions like the IEC South Africa to ensure a safe, informed, and authentic election experience for our community,” TikTok’s Government Relations and Public Policy Lead for Southern Africa, Tholoana Ncheke-Mahlaela, said.

“Information integrity is fundamental to the credibility of any democratic process. In an increasingly complex digital environment, protecting voters from misinformation and disinformation requires coordinated action across institutions, technology platforms, civil society and citizens themselves.

“This partnership represents an important commitment to ensuring that South Africans can access accurate, trustworthy election information and participate in the 2026 Local Government Elections with confidence,” Moxii Africa Director William Bird welcoming the partnership.

Bird said he is proud to support this collective effort to strengthen trust, transparency and democratic resilience.

Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

text:
THE STARLINK QUESTION INDIA MUST ASK 🇮🇳

Why is Elon Musk pushing so aggressively to enter India’s satellite internet market?

Is this merely a business battle—or a question of DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY?

FOLLOW THE MONEY. FOLLOW THE TECHNOLOGY.

Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service. SpaceX also operates Starshield, a separate programme serving US national security customers.

In March 2024, Reuters reported a classified $1.8 BILLION contract involving SpaceX and America’s National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), an intelligence agency responsible for satellite-based reconnaissance.

The programme reportedly involves a network of satellites designed to enhance Earth observation and intelligence capabilities.

Reuters report:
https://t.co/IknOaaml55

Starlink and Starshield are NOT the same service. But both belong to the SpaceX ecosystem.

That raises legitimate strategic questions for every country considering foreign satellite infrastructure.

Who operates the network?
Who controls its software and updates?
Who governs access during a geopolitical crisis?
What happens when commercial interests collide with national interests?

These are questions of NATIONAL SECURITY, not anti-technology paranoia.

DATA IS THE NEW STRATEGIC TERRITORY.

Satellite internet can generate operational and subscriber information, including connection records and network metadata. Such information can have commercial value and, depending on the circumstances, potential intelligence value.

This does NOT prove that Starlink is handing Indian user data to US intelligence agencies.

But India must establish clear, enforceable safeguards for DATA PRIVACY, CYBERSECURITY and NATIONAL SECURITY before any foreign provider scales up.

ASK UKRAINE WHAT NETWORK DEPENDENCE CAN MEAN.

The Russia–Ukraine war has demonstrated how commercial satellite connectivity can become strategically important during a conflict.

When a private company controls a critical communications capability, its technical decisions can have consequences far beyond business.

India must ask a fundamental question: Can we maintain secure, uninterrupted communications when our national interests are at stake?

STRATEGIC AUTONOMY demands that we plan for that possibility.

INDIA IS NOT A TECHNOLOGICAL DESERT.

India has built a vast mobile communications ecosystem, expanded fibre connectivity and invested in indigenous telecom technology.

The answer is not to reject foreign technology automatically. It is to ensure that SATELLITE INTERNET complements India’s infrastructure without creating avoidable strategic dependencies.

REGULATION IS NOT THE SAME AS CONTROL.

A government can license a foreign company, impose security conditions and establish compliance requirements. But technical control also depends on network architecture, encryption, software access, operational authority and the ability to enforce national laws.

India needs independently verifiable safeguards, robust lawful-access procedures, incident-response mechanisms and credible contingency plans.

DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY must be more than a policy slogan.

FAIR COMPETITION. EQUAL RULES. STRONG SECURITY.

India must not allow domestic monopolies to suppress innovation. Equally, commercial pressure must never weaken national security safeguards.

The real question is not whether India should welcome Starlink. Satellite internet could benefit millions of Indians. The question is whether any foreign company should become indispensable to critical Indian communications without strong sovereign safeguards.

Affordable connectivity.
Competition and innovation.
Indian data protection.
Secure infrastructure.
Enforceable regulatory oversight.

India must welcome technology on INDIAN TERMS.

THE BOTTOM LINE 🇮🇳

This is bigger than Elon Musk versus India’s telecom giants. India must never confuse access to technology with control over technology.

text:
1/ From FY22-23 to FY24-25, India collected ₹1,096 crore in crypto TDS.

Meanwhile, uncollected TDS since the regime began in July 2022 is estimated at ~₹19,049 crore.

The reason: ~95% of Indian crypto trading now happens on offshore platforms that deduct no TDS, around ₹9 lakh crore in FY25-26 alone. Factoring in capital gains tax, the estimated loss to the exchequer is ~₹57,147 crore, and it's growing every year.

A recent TIOL Knowledge Foundation report says fixing the tax design, rather than more enforcement against a shrinking base, could bring in up to ₹1.81 lakh crore in capital gains tax over 5 years. 

Sharing some interesting insights from the report below.  🧵

4/ Root cause #1: the 1% TDS makes following the rules the expensive option

>Every transaction on an Indian exchange attracts a 1% TDS. Active traders feel that cost on every trade, while offshore platforms deduct nothing.
>So volume moves offshore, mostly through P2P (peer-to-peer) trading.

5/ Root cause #2: a legal gap offshore platforms rely on
In P2P trading. An offshore platform matches buyers and sellers, but the rupees move directly between Indian bank accounts. Because the platform isn't registered in India and never handles the money, it argues it has no duty to deduct TDS.

That's why blocking websites alone didn't work. When FIU-IND blocked 25 offshore exchanges in Oct'25, users didn't come back to Indian exchanges. They moved to P2P on platforms that were still accessible.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

I had the opportunity to learn about the First Amendment (my fav)and the importance of a free press through Kevin Goldberg, First Amendment Specialist at the Freedom Forum, who discusses the role of a free press in a democratic society and the constitutional protections that safeguard it in the United States.

The First Amendment protects five fundamental freedoms,religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and the right to petition the government. These freedoms enable citizens to question authority, express dissent, expose injustice, and hold those in power accountable. A free press, in particular, is indispensable to democracy because it informs the public and scrutinises the exercise of power.

The Freedom Forum is a financially independent, non-partisan, international organisation dedicated to free press, free speech, and free spirit for all people. Through educational programmes, conferences, publishing, broadcasting, training, research, and partnerships, it works to advance these freedoms.

My visit to the United States Capitol brought these ideas into sharper focus. For someone committed to human rights and social justice, the First Amendment offers an important reminder that democracy is about more than elections and institutions. It is also about protecting the right to question, dissent, organise, and demand accountability.

For India, the question is not merely whether these freedoms exist in the Constitution, but how effectively they are protected in practice. The freedom of journalists to scrutinise governments, the right of citizens to criticise those in power, and the ability of marginalised communities to make their voices heard are essential to a functioning democracy.

A democracy is only as meaningful as the freedoms its people can exercise,including the freedom to question those who govern.

WHEN A CREATOR SPEAKS UP, DOES HER VOICE BECOME THE TARGET? DIGITAL CENSORSHIP, META RESTRICTIONS AND THE RIGHT TO BE HEARD

A creator behind @the.ranting.gola has shared a disturbing account of restrictions on her Facebook activity. In her video, she says she cannot go LIVE for a year, send messages, post videos to her broadcast group or share videos to her Story. She also describes monetisation being unavailable and some content becoming inaccessible in India.

She says she had made a video supporting Neha Singh Rathore and opposing ABVP-related groups. According to her account, she was not clearly informed which specific post had triggered the restrictions and had to investigate the matter herself.

These are the creator’s allegations and account of her experience. The precise reason for the restrictions, the applicable Meta policy and whether a government direction was involved have not been independently established from this video alone.

But her experience raises a fundamental democratic question: What happens when ordinary citizens and independent creators lose their ability to communicate with their audiences without receiving a clear explanation?

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED CONCERN

Recent reporting in India makes these questions particularly urgent.

• ThePrint, 19 October 2026: Reported on a MeitY advisory asking Meta to review its Facebook and Instagram recommendation systems, alongside restrictions affecting posts and accounts connected with protests and political events.

https://t.co/QeWUIIrGmC

• Alt News, 15 October 2026: Documented restrictions affecting journalists and media organisations covering the Delhi protests, including cases in which Meta notices cited automated enforcement or government and law-enforcement requests.

https://t.co/1RjkoJX1nE

• Reporters Without Borders: Reported a broader rise in restrictions affecting journalistic content in India during 2026, raising concerns about opaque takedown processes and the public’s right to information.

https://t.co/g6FhmAUglC

These reports provide important context. They do not, by themselves, establish that this particular creator was restricted at the government's request. That question deserves a direct, evidence-based answer.

THE REAL ISSUE: TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

Social media companies have the right to enforce legitimate community standards. But enforcement must be proportionate, transparent and open to meaningful appeal.

If a creator is prohibited from going LIVE for an entire year, the platform should explain:

Which specific post, video or action triggered the restriction?
Which rule was allegedly violated, and what evidence supports that decision?
Was the action taken under Meta's own policies, an automated system or a government/legal request?
Why were such extensive restrictions imposed, and what appeal and restoration mechanisms are available?

A vague account-status notification is not an adequate substitute for a meaningful explanation.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY ELECTIONS

Democracy also depends on the freedom to question power, criticise political organisations, support dissenting voices and share information without arbitrary punishment.

When restrictions disproportionately affect people discussing political controversies, the public deserves to know whether the cause is legitimate policy enforcement, automated error, coordinated reporting or an external legal direction. These possibilities must be investigated rather than assumed.

Our demand is simple: transparency from Meta, accountability from any authority that seeks unlawful restrictions, and equal protection for every citizen's right to express a political opinion.

No creator should have to guess why their voice has been restricted. No government should be allowed to silence lawful criticism through opaque processes. And no technology company should be permitted to hide consequential decisions behind unexplained notifications.

If the restrictions were justified, publish the reasons. If they were mistaken or unlawful, restore the affected rights. Let evidence decide—not political loyalty.

text:
The man grabbed me by the hair at 2:15 in the morning because I refused to give him the front seat of a military shuttle. He was Major Thomas Vance, a powerful officer at Fort Marshall, and he believed I was nothing more than a civilian wife who needed to learn her place. What he didn't know was that in seventy-two hours, he would be standing in formation while my name was announced as the new commander of his entire base.

The pain hit before I understood what he had done. One second I was sitting near the front because a severe migraine made the motion of the old shuttle harder to tolerate, and the next my head snapped backward as his fist closed around my hair. My shoulder struck a metal rail, but I managed to catch myself before falling to the dirty floor. Vance stood over me smiling, as if humiliating a stranger in front of his subordinates was entertainment.

“I told you to move, sweetheart,” he said. “This is my seat.” There was no reserved sign, no regulation, and no reason he needed that particular seat except that everyone around him had apparently learned to treat it like his private throne. He smelled of beer, and a heavy gold challenge coin clicked across his fingers while two younger officers watched from several rows away.

I could have told him exactly who I was. At forty-two, I had recently been promoted to colonel, and my official change-of-command ceremony was scheduled for Monday morning at 0800. I had arrived three days early, under my maiden name and wearing an old gray hoodie, because I wanted to see Fort Marshall before its leaders had time to polish everything for my arrival. If I had shown him my identification, his whole attitude would have changed instantly.

That was exactly why I stayed silent.

Vance leaned closer and called me a “dep enda,” the insulting nickname some people use for military spouses. Then he told me I was “breathing his air” and threatened to have the military police remove me from the installation if I didn't move. I looked him straight in the eye and said, “I'm not moving.” That was when he put his hand in my hair and dragged me from the seat.

For one second, every instinct I had developed through years of military service told me to put him on the floor. I knew how to break his grip, control his arm, and end the confrontation before his two friends could even stand. But something stopped me. It wasn't fear—it was the sight of the people behind him.

A young sergeant named Maya Lin sat several rows back holding a battered backpack against her chest. She was staring at her lap while picking at the skin around her fingernails until one of them bled. Earlier, when Vance boarded, I had watched him stop beside her and threaten to put her on weekend guard duty if reports he assigned at 1800 weren't flawless. Maya had shrunk into her seat before he even raised his voice.

At the wheel sat Chief Warrant Officer David Miller. He had watched Vance put his hands on me through the rearview mirror, but he never stopped the shuttle or said a word. His knuckles had turned white around the steering wheel, and I realized he wasn't indifferent. He was afraid.

That was when I understood Fort Marshall's real problem.

Vance wasn't simply an arrogant major having a bad night. He behaved this way because years of silence had convinced him he could. The younger officers laughed when he mocked people, the senior people protected him, and frightened soldiers like Maya had learned that speaking up might hurt them more than staying quiet. Punishing Vance alone would not be enough if the culture that created him stayed intact.

So when he said, “I don't ask for things. I take them,” I looked at him for three long seconds and answered, “Okay.”

Then I picked up my bag and walked toward the rear.

He laughed behind me. “Finally. Civilian wives sometimes think they own the damn military.” One of the junior officers congratulated him for showing me “who's boss,” and Vance dropped into the front seat like a man settling onto a throne. I kept walking until I reached Maya.

She was still staring at her bleeding finger. I pulled a clean tissue from my pocket, placed it gently on her backpack, and waited until she looked up. She expected to see someone humiliated, but I gave her only a calm nod. I wanted her to understand one thing without me saying it aloud: I see you.

At the back of the shuttle, I took out my phone and opened an encrypted notes application. I recorded Vance's name, the time, the apparent intoxication, the physical contact, his exact words, and every witness I could identify. My scalp still hurt, my migraine was pounding, and the cold air leaking through the emergency exit cut through my jeans. But for the first time that night, I smiled.

I had come to Fort Marshall because of another young soldier.

Private First Class Chloe Davies had been nineteen when she died by suicide six months earlier. Before her death, she wrote her mother a letter describing bullying, humiliation, interference with mental health care, and leaders who taught soldiers that complaining only made things worse. One name appeared repeatedly in the material I reviewed before taking this assignment.

Major Thomas Vance.

I had spent nearly every favor I possessed getting myself assigned to Fort Marshall after reading Chloe's letter. Senior generals warned me the installation was a “snake pit” where entrenched leaders protected one another. I told them to send me anyway. What I hadn't expected was for one of the men I already planned to examine to personally demonstrate his behavior before I had even officially arrived.

When the shuttle finally stopped, Vance walked past me and gave a mocking little salute. “Try not to get lost, sweetheart.” I looked at him and answered, “I'll do my best.” He walked away without realizing he had just handed his future commander a firsthand account of exactly what she had come to investigate.

Then Maya approached me.

“You didn't do anything wrong,” she whispered.

I told her she didn't owe me an apology for being afraid of someone who had taught her there were consequences for challenging him. But before she could ask who I really was, Chief Miller walked toward us and quietly admitted that he had seen everything. When I asked whether he would still say that when telling the truth became inconvenient, his face changed.

He nodded.

And less than twelve hours later, I would discover that Vance was already moving to punish the one witness he thought was weakest.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.
